items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

Codex App on Windows. This request concerns skill eligibility for ordinary subagents and should apply consistently wherever Codex supports them.

### What feature would you like to see?

Add a native per-skill policy that keeps a skill available to the main/root agent while making it unavailable for automatic selection and explicit invocation by all subagents, including nested descendants.

This should work with ordinary subagents, without defining custom agents, overriding built-in agent roles, or maintaining separate configuration files for workers. An optional scope in `agents/openai.yaml` would make the restriction travel with the skill. Existing behavior should remain the default.

The concrete use case is an orchestration/recovery skill that resumes existing workers after an interruption. I want the main agent to select that skill automatically, while workers continue their own assignments without independently initiating recovery or orchestration. Recursive orchestration or delegation is a concern motivating the request; I am not reporting an observed recursive-spawning bug.

Expected behavior:

- A main-only skill remains available for both automatic selection and explicit invocation by the main/root agent.
- That skill is excluded from subagents' automatically supplied skill catalogs, and explicit skill invocation from a subagent is rejected by Codex.
- The restriction covers ordinary children, nested descendants, and resumed subagent threads.
- Other skills and normal subagent operation remain available.
- Eligibility is enforced by Codex's skill discovery/invocation paths. Existing filesystem sandbox rules can remain unchanged.

Setting `allow_implicit_invocation: false` does not provide this distinction: it also removes automatic selection for the main agent. A sentence in `SKILL.md` telling subagents not to use the skill is an instruction rather than an enforced eligibility rule.

### Additional information

The current [skill-policy documentation](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/build-skills#optional-metadata) documents `allow_implicit_invocation`, but no main-agent/subagent scope.

Source checked at [`d83bb540ec64bf6b009bca0283b0be91ea33f26a`](https://github.com/openai/codex/commit/d83bb540ec64bf6b009bca0283b0be91ea33f26a) on 2026-10-07:

- [`SkillPolicy`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/d83bb540ec64bf6b009bca0283b0be91ea33f26a/codex-rs/skills/src/model.rs#L63-L68) contains the implicit-invocation flag and product metadata, without a main-agent/subagent selector.
- [Child configuration](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/d83bb540ec64bf6b009bca0283b0be91ea33f26a/codex-rs/core/src/agent/child_config.rs#L131-L156) starts from a clone of the parent's configuration.
- [Host skill catalog construction](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/d83bb540ec64bf6b009bca0283b0be91ea33f26a/codex-rs/ext/skills/src/provider/host.rs#L146-L167) applies skill enablement and implicit-invocation visibility, without this distinction.

Related requests:

- [#42440](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/42440) proposes host-selected per-thread automatic catalogs while preserving explicit invocation of hidden skills.
- [#26806](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/26806) scopes inherited personal/project instructions rather than skill eligibility.
- [#30967](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/30967) proposes host-controlled per-thread skill/plugin selection.

This request is for a skill-owned main/root-only eligibility policy that automatically covers ordinary descendants, without custom agent definitions or per-thread host integration.

items.title: Roll back stale Guardian reviews before reusing reviewer history
items.body:
Roll back stale Guardian reviews before reusing reviewer history

## Why

Authorization updates during a pending Guardian approval can invalidate its decision. Retries need the updated guidance without inheriting the invalidated review or losing earlier valid context.

## What changed

- Validate authorization while the reviewer is reserved, before publishing its history checkpoint.
- Roll back stale attempts to the last committed review, preserving earlier valid reviews across repeated invalidations.
- Pin the issuing action's repository instruction snapshot for reviewers and retries, avoiding fresh instruction discovery through disconnected executors.
- Treat stale authorization as a request for a new review rather than a failed decision.

## Testing

Add regression coverage for repeated approval invalidation, retention of earlier valid context, exclusion of stale decisions, and execution of the pending action exactly once. Extend the disconnected-executor test to verify that retries retain repository instructions and use updated authorization.

#### Runtime evidence

Observation date: **2026-10-07**. All times below are **UTC**.

For the launch whose first diagnostic entry is **12:26:37.131**:

- **12:26:40.681:** durable WebSocket initialization succeeds; handshake duration **95 ms**.
- **12:26:40.900:** `thread/list` succeeds; response duration **218 ms**, queue wait **454 ms**.
- **12:26:43.187–12:28:28.907:** **261 distinct failed background read request IDs targeting 29 distinct threads**, across two renderers.
- Those failures have `method=thread/read`, `source=thread_hydration`, `priority=background`, `error.code=-32003`, `error.message="thread access denied"`, and `failureReason=null`. Queue waits are **0–1 ms**.
- **12:29:34:** an explicit built-in direct read of one of those same denied targets succeeds, returning the same ID, host `durable`, and one turn of history.

A separate earlier launch at **12:24:55.901** recorded **143 distinct failed read request IDs across the same count of 29 target threads**, with the same denial signature. Counts are method-specific request counts, not model turns, user clicks, or unique task counts.

Selected fields from one failure, with identifiers removed:

```text
method=thread/read
source=thread_hydration
priority=background
error={"code":-32003,"message":"thread access denied"}
failureReason=null
durationMs=109
queueWaitMs=0
```

These observations establish successful listing plus a failing background read path. They do not establish queue saturation, lost cloud data, or why the backend rejects those reads.

#### Installed-client investigation lead — not a confirmed root cause

Read-only inspection of the installed build found a concrete difference between ordinary metadata reads and explicit shared direct reads:

- The durable transport in `main-B6ZOwXa3.js` can intercept a normal `thread/read` and perform HTTP `GET /v1/threads/{id}` with a **30-second** timeout.
- Its strict params schema does not include `threadAccess`. Explicit `params.threadAccess="shared"` therefore takes the WebSocket path.
- Native catalog/direct-ID reads explicitly use shared access for the durable host.
- Another outgoing-message path can infer shared access and put `threadAccess="shared"` on the JSON-RPC **top level**. The HTTP parser accepts the message but strips that additional top-level field, so inferred shared and explicit shared can select different transports.
- A synthetic parser check using the installed schema/library confirmed this selection difference. It is not a trace of the actual failing requests.
- The sidebar metadata query has `retry:1` and `staleTime:60000`. A lower-level hydration path uses at most two concurrent reads and skips applying a failed result. That skip does not prove deletion of existing entries or explain the entire sidebar outcome.

Please compare the actual failing background request with the successful direct read, including transport, shared-access propagation, account/product context, and subsequent catalog/sidebar reconciliation. The wire payload and server-side authorization decisions have not been captured.

#### Related reports checked before filing

- [#51572](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/51572) reports repeated access-denied background hydration on **Windows**. This macOS report adds the missing cloud-sidebar outcome, Dots/listing contrast, same-target successful direct history read, and individual-entry recovery.
- [#49121](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/49121) concerns missing **ChatGPT-linked project rows** while local projects remain. This report concerns durable **task entries**, with a different observed read-denial signature.

A shared root cause has not been established; please consolidate if appropriate.

Only sanitized versions, aggregate counts, timing, and selected diagnostic fields are included. No private task IDs/titles, request IDs, account identifiers, home paths, conversation contents, credentials, screenshots, or raw logs are attached. No local database, credentials, settings, or installed-app modifications were made during diagnosis.

### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

26.930.61225

### What subscription do you have?

ChatGPT Pro

### What platform is your computer?

Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26300.0 x64

### What issue are you seeing?

After a recent ChatGPT/Codex Windows Desktop update, my STM32 embedded-development workflow stopped working correctly inside Codex.

The exact same STM32CubeIDE installation, GNU Arm toolchain, OpenOCD, ST-LINK devices, serial ports, TCP connections, and firmware projects continue to work normally outside Codex.

Current bundled Codex CLI version: 0.160.1.
The same core problem was also reproduced with Codex CLI 0.160.0.

The most serious problem is that STM32CubeIDE's bundled GNU Arm GCC no longer starts inside Codex.

Running:

    arm-none-eabi-gcc.exe --version

works normally from standard Windows PowerShell.

Inside Codex it fails immediately with Windows error 623:

    ERROR_ILLEGAL_DLL_RELOCATION
    "Illegal DLL relocation"

Windows reports an error equivalent to:

    A system DLL was relocated in memory.
    The DLL occupied an address range reserved for Windows NT system DLLs.

The compiler does not even reach the point of printing its version.

The same failure also occurs when GCC is launched indirectly through Python subprocess.

STM32CubeIDE's bundled OpenOCD also fails during startup with the same DLL relocation class of error.

Therefore the problem is not specific to GCC.

There is also an important control case:

In another STM32 firmware project, Codex first attempted to build the original STM32CubeIDE GNU Arm GCC project, but GCC failed because of the DLL relocation error.

Codex then modified that firmware project's build configuration so that the project could be built using Clang/LLVM instead of GNU Arm GCC.

After converting the project to Clang/LLVM, Codex successfully:

- ran the Clang/LLVM toolchain,
- completed the firmware build,
- and completed the associated static tests without errors.

Therefore:

    Original STM32CubeIDE / GNU Arm GCC project
        -> GNU Arm GCC
        -> ERROR_ILLEGAL_DLL_RELOCATION / error 623
        -> build cannot start

    Project modified by Codex for Clang/LLVM
        -> Clang/LLVM
        -> firmware build succeeds
        -> static tests succeed

This shows that native compilation and test execution in general are not broken. The failure appears selective to certain executables/DLL/runtime combinations or their interaction with the current Windows Codex sandbox/process-mitigation environment.

The ASLR mitigation settings are also different.

Normal user PowerShell:

    ForceRelocateImages : OFF
    RequireInfo         : OFF
    BottomUp            : ON
    HighEntropy         : ON

Codex execution environment:

    ForceRelocateImages : ON
    RequireInfo         : ON
    BottomUp            : ON
    HighEntropy         : ON

I also tested all three permission modes exposed by the Codex Windows Desktop UI:

    Ask for approval
    Approve for me
    workspace-safe

All three modes produce exactly the same mitigation configuration:

    ForceRelocateImages : ON
    RequireInfo         : ON
    BottomUp            : ON
    HighEntropy         : ON

and all three produce the same GNU Arm GCC "Illegal DLL relocation" failure.

Therefore the problem does not appear to be caused by the selected approval mode.

There are additional regressions in the same environment:

- COM10: Access Denied
- COM12: Access Denied
- TCP connections that previously worked: Access Denied

The same COM ports and TCP connections work normally outside Codex.

Two connected ST-LINK V3 devices also expose removable FAT volumes:

    D: STLINK_V3S
    E: STLINK_V3M

Both are fully readable from normal Windows PowerShell.

However, Codex/MXC can fail with:

    Filesystem path 'D:\' (readonlyPaths) could not be resolved to a filesystem object.

    Because deniedPaths are present, MXC cannot verify it does not alias a denied object and rejects the config.

This can prevent AGENTS.md from loading and can prevent an existing Codex conversation from being resumed.

As another control test, VS Code Agent on the exact same Windows PC can successfully:

- build STM32CubeIDE GNU Arm GCC projects,
- access ST-LINK,
- and communicate with the hardware.

The Windows AppX deployment history shows that OpenAI.Codex_26.930.2377.0 was installed on October 2, 2026, and the STM32 workflow still worked correctly later that same day.

After subsequent ChatGPT/Codex Windows Desktop updates, these failures appeared.

Nothing in the STM32 development environment was intentionally changed.

This appears to be a regression in the Windows Codex sandbox/process-launch/runtime layer rather than an STM32CubeIDE configuration problem.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

The core GCC/OpenOCD issue can be reproduced without any proprietary firmware project.

Reproduction for GNU Arm GCC:

1. On Windows 11 x64, install STM32CubeIDE.

2. Locate STM32CubeIDE's bundled arm-none-eabi-gcc.exe.

3. Open a normal user PowerShell window and run:

    & "FULL_PATH_TO_ARM_GCC\arm-none-eabi-gcc.exe" --version

Expected/observed result outside Codex:

    GCC starts normally and prints its version.

4. In ChatGPT/Codex Windows Desktop, ask Codex to execute the exact same command:

    & "FULL_PATH_TO_ARM_GCC\arm-none-eabi-gcc.exe" --version

Observed result inside Codex:

    ERROR_ILLEGAL_DLL_RELOCATION
    Windows error 623

    A system DLL was relocated in memory.
    The DLL occupied an address range reserved for Windows NT system DLLs.

No GCC version is printed because the executable fails during startup.

5. Repeat with STM32CubeIDE's bundled OpenOCD:

Normal PowerShell:

    & "FULL_PATH_TO_OPENOCD\openocd.exe" --version

Result:

    Works normally.

Codex:

    & "FULL_PATH_TO_OPENOCD\openocd.exe" --version

Result:

    Fails during startup with the same DLL relocation class of error.

6. Compare ASLR process mitigation settings.

Normal PowerShell:

    (Get-ProcessMitigation -Id $PID).ASLR |
        Format-List ForceRelocateImages,RequireInfo,BottomUp,HighEntropy

Result:

    ForceRelocateImages : OFF
    RequireInfo         : OFF
    BottomUp            : ON
    HighEntropy         : ON

Run the same command from Codex.

Result:

    ForceRelocateImages : ON
    RequireInfo         : ON
    BottomUp            : ON
    HighEntropy         : ON

7. Repeat the Codex GCC test under all three Desktop permission modes:

    Ask for approval
    Approve for me
    workspace-safe

All three modes produce:

    ForceRelocateImages : ON
    RequireInfo         : ON
    BottomUp            : ON
    HighEntropy         : ON

and all three reproduce the same GNU Arm GCC DLL relocation failure.

8. Additional control test:

In another STM32 firmware project, allow Codex to replace the GNU Arm GCC build configuration with a Clang/LLVM build configuration.

Observed:

    Clang/LLVM executes successfully.
    The modified firmware project builds successfully.
    Static tests complete successfully.

This demonstrates that Codex can execute a complete compiler/build/test workflow, while GNU Arm GCC and OpenOCD fail selectively.

9. Serial reproduction:

Attempt to access serial ports previously accessible from Codex:

    COM10
    COM12

Observed inside Codex:

    Access Denied

Observed outside Codex:

    Both ports work normally.

10. TCP reproduction:

Attempt the same TCP connection that previously worked in Codex.

Observed inside Codex:

    Access Denied

Observed outside Codex:

    Connection works normally.

11. MXC / removable-drive reproduction:

Connect ST-LINK V3 devices that expose removable FAT volumes:

    D: STLINK_V3S
    E: STLINK_V3M

Verify in normal PowerShell:

    Test-Path D:\
    Test-Path E:\
    Get-ChildItem D:\
    Get-ChildItem E:\

These work normally.

Then start/resume the Codex session.

Codex/MXC may fail before command execution with an error similar to:

    Filesystem path 'D:\' (readonlyPaths) could not be resolved to a filesystem object.

    Because deniedPaths are present, MXC cannot verify it does not alias a denied object and rejects the config.

This may prevent AGENTS.md from loading or prevent the conversation from being resumed.

Control environment:

The same Windows machine and STM32 tools work correctly when used from normal PowerShell and from VS Code Agent.

Known-good state:

OpenAI.Codex_26.930.2377.0 was installed on October 2, 2026, and this STM32 workflow still worked correctly later that day.

The failures appeared after subsequent Codex Windows Desktop updates.

### Summary

In a Codex desktop conversation backed by a managed Linux/cloud execution environment, the agent receives native thread inspection and handoff-status tools but no callable thread creation, fork, or handoff operation. The user explicitly requests continuing the work in a new Codex session, but the assistant cannot perform the operation.

Observed on 2026-10-07. Desktop build, subscription, and OS version were not verified. This is a report of the live tool surface, not an identified root cause.

### Observed tool surface

Present in the live tool catalog:
- `codex_app__get_handoff_status`
- `codex_app__list_threads`
- `codex_app__read_thread`
- `codex_app__wait_threads`
- `codex_app__list_projects`
- `codex_app__set_thread_title`
- `codex_app__set_thread_archived`

Absent from the live catalog:
- `codex_app__handoff_thread`
- `codex_app__create_thread`
- `codex_app__fork_thread`

The agent also checked the callable runtime object directly:

```js
typeof tools.codex_app__handoff_thread // "undefined"
typeof tools.codex_app__create_thread  // "undefined"
typeof tools.codex_app__fork_thread    // "undefined"
typeof tools.tool_search              // "undefined"
```

The catalog was inspected again after the user corrected the assistant; the operations remained absent. `list_threads` successfully returned threads and sidebar state. No handoff operation was invoked, no operation ID was created, and no handoff error or approval rejection occurred.

### Reproduction / observed sequence

1. Use a Codex desktop conversation backed by managed cloud execution.
2. Ask the assistant to hand off the work to a new session in Codex.
3. Inspect the native tool catalog and callable runtime surface.
4. Observe that handoff status and thread readers are exposed, but creation/fork/handoff and a discovery path are missing.
5. The assistant can only produce a manual text handoff instead of creating the requested continuation.

The user reports that the native handoff operation has worked before. A controlled comparison against that previous session was not captured, so no last-known-good build or version regression is claimed.

### Expected behavior

Provide a supported way to create a continuation session or hand off the current work when the user explicitly requests it.

If these operations are intentionally unavailable from a managed cloud session, expose a structured capability reason and a supported desktop continuation route. Availability guidance should distinguish an operation that exists in the product from an operation that is unavailable to the current agent.

The handoff-status tool should not be the only exposed handoff capability without any explanation of how an operation can be started.

### Assistant behavior improvement

The assistant initially misread the user's Portuguese request for a new session as a sidebar section request, then stated too broadly that no tool existed. The user had to clarify that they meant Codex itself and that handoff is native.

Improve interpretation of continuation requests and capability reporting:
- Recognize requests for a new session/chat as thread continuation, including minor spelling variations.
- Say "not exposed in this session" when that is the evidence, rather than implying the native product feature does not exist.
- Provide an actionable native recovery route instead of repeatedly asking the user to copy context manually.

### Related reports

- #42973: remote/headless sessions lose creation, messaging, fork, and handoff tools while readers remain available.
- #29223: missing thread-management tools in fresh sessions.
- #35283: native handoff operation lacks parity with the desktop UI.
- #49770: a fresh desktop thread omits native cross-thread tools.

This report adds the managed-cloud case, the available `get_handoff_status` / missing `handoff_thread` mismatch, and the resulting misleading assistant guidance.

### Privacy

No private repository details, work artifacts, conversation identifiers, full transcripts, credentials, or screenshots are included.

### What issue are you seeing?

I am seeing several issues when using Codex on very large, long-running software projects.

For context, I am a heavy user of both Codex and Claude Code and have been using coding agents extensively for approximately two years. I currently use them on multiple large projects in parallel, including repositories/projects exceeding 1M lines of code. My typical workflow involves long-running sessions, persistent repository-level governance, multiple sub-agents, worktrees, audits, implementation tasks, and continuous progression toward a defined product goal.

The main issues I have observed are:

1. **Critical worktree lifecycle / safety issue**

   In one recent case, Codex deleted the main project worktree.

   The repository was under Git, so part of the damage was recoverable, but some uncommitted work was lost and I had to recover additional files from a Time Machine backup.

   More generally, worktree lifecycle management is unreliable in long-running sessions.

   I explicitly define rules such as:

   - agents may create temporary worktrees;
   - they are responsible for integrating their changes;
   - they must clean up the worktree afterward;
   - they must never delete or damage the primary working tree.

   These rules are present in multiple persistent governance locations in the repository, including AGENTS.md and project governance files.

   Despite this, Codex sometimes creates worktrees without properly completing their lifecycle. Over time I have ended up with a very large amount of stale worktree/cache data, on the order of ~100 GB.

   The primary-worktree deletion is obviously the most serious occurrence because this moves beyond inefficiency into potential data loss.

2. **Delegation is far too conservative with GPT-6.1 Sol / Ultra**

   My orchestrator runs GPT-6.1 Sol at Ultra reasoning, with explicit instructions to delegate aggressively when tasks are parallelizable.

   In practice, Codex generally uses only around 1-3 agents concurrently, and I rarely observe more than approximately 6 agents being used effectively.

   This remains true even when the backlog contains many clearly independent tasks that could safely execute in parallel.

   This creates a significant throughput problem on large projects.

   By comparison, Claude Code / Claude Ultra is able to fan out much more aggressively in similar workflows. I can run very large sequences of agent tasks, sometimes hundreds of agent executions over the lifetime of a job, while still observing visible incremental progress.

   I am not necessarily asking Codex to blindly spawn 100 agents simultaneously. The issue is that its current orchestration appears excessively conservative even when the repository and task graph provide substantial safe parallelism.

3. **Sub-agent model selection rules are not consistently respected**

   I explicitly define routing rules for sub-agents, for example which tasks should use Luna versus Sol and which reasoning level should be used.

   These model-selection rules are not consistently followed.

   This makes it difficult to optimize the workflow for cost, latency and task complexity, because the orchestrator sometimes chooses a different model than the repository governance explicitly requests.

4. **Instruction adherence appears to degrade during long sessions / after compaction**

   Long-running sessions appear to progressively lose adherence to repository governance and previous decisions.

   Important rules are persisted in the repository rather than existing only in chat context, but Codex does not appear to reliably re-anchor itself on those files after long sessions or compaction.

   This is especially noticeable for:

   - worktree lifecycle rules;
   - model-routing rules;
   - delegation requirements;
   - project governance/state;
   - previously established implementation decisions.

   This suggests that compaction may preserve a high-level summary while losing operationally important constraints.

5. **Compaction is expensive and long sessions become increasingly inefficient**

   On GPT-6.1 Sol / Ultra, compaction can take several minutes in my experience, sometimes roughly 5-8 minutes.

   More importantly, after a session has accumulated substantial context and undergone multiple compactions, the session often feels materially less effective.

   The agent continues working, but the ratio between compute/time spent and actual repository progress becomes poor.

   I often see repeated auditing, rediscovery, conservative planning, or re-evaluation of already-known information instead of a steady increase in completed implementation.

6. **Limited visible progress over multi-day autonomous development**

   This is harder to quantify as a strict bug, but it is one of the most important practical problems.

   When running Codex intensively for approximately five working days on a large repository, I often do not see a proportional amount of completed product progress relative to the amount of compute and agent time consumed.

   With comparable Claude Code workflows, I generally observe more visible incremental wins: features completed, tests passing, backlog items closed, integrations completed, and repository state converging toward the target.

   With Codex, long sessions can spend a significant amount of time reasoning, auditing, compacting, and rediscovering state without producing an equivalent amount of merged implementation.

My impression is that these problems are related rather than completely independent:

**long session → context growth → compaction → operational instruction loss → conservative orchestration → repeated rediscovery/auditing → limited delegation → low implementation throughput.**

The worktree issue additionally indicates that safety-critical repository invariants are not always being preserved across this process.

I would be happy to provide additional logs, thread IDs, sanitized governance files, examples of AGENTS.md / goal instructions, worktree state, or discuss the workflow directly with the Codex team.

I am probably an unusually heavy Codex user, so my workloads may expose orchestration and long-context issues that are less visible in smaller repositories or shorter sessions.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Uploaded thread: 01a113b7-b612-7e71-840b-54ef46a0c746

### What is the expected behavior?

For large and long-running projects, I would expect Codex to preserve the same operational reliability that it has near the beginning of a session.

Specifically:

- **Repository safety invariants should be absolute.**
  The primary worktree should never be deleted or destructively modified as part of temporary worktree cleanup.

- **Agents that create worktrees should own their lifecycle.**
  Creation, implementation, integration/merge, verification and cleanup should be treated as one lifecycle rather than leaving stale worktrees behind.

- **Persistent repository instructions should survive compaction.**
  Important rules stored in AGENTS.md or equivalent governance files should remain authoritative throughout the session and should be re-read/revalidated when necessary after compaction.

- **Explicit model-routing rules should be respected.**
  If the project specifies Luna for one category of task and Sol for another, the orchestrator should either follow those rules or clearly explain why it cannot.

- **Delegation should scale with available independent work.**
  When 10, 20 or more genuinely independent tasks exist, the orchestrator should be capable of exploiting substantially more parallelism instead of routinely executing only 1-3 sub-agents.

- **Compaction should preserve operational state, not only conversational meaning.**
  Decisions, invariants, active tasks, worktree ownership, implementation state and governance constraints need to survive compaction reliably.

- **Long sessions should continue converging toward the goal.**
  The agent should progressively convert backlog items into implemented, tested and integrated changes rather than increasingly spending time on repeated discovery, planning and auditing.

- **Progress should be measurable and persistent.**
  For very large autonomous jobs, Codex would benefit from maintaining a durable representation of completed actions, active tasks, implementation status, decisions, failures and pending work rather than relying primarily on conversational context.

The high-level expectation is that a five-day autonomous development run should behave like a continuous engineering process, not like a sequence of partially amnesiac sessions.

For very large repositories, I would expect compaction to make the context smaller while preserving the operational state required to continue working safely and efficiently.

### Additional information

I am happy to discuss this in more detail with the Codex team. I use both Codex and Claude Code at unusually high volume, including large repositories, long-running sessions, parallel agents and persistent project governance, so I can provide comparative feedback and real-world examples if that is useful.

## Result

Native Chrome control is not restored. Selecting Chrome explicitly in the composer (`@Chrome`, browser family `chrome`) still fails before the browser runtime initializes or reaches the extension handshake. No page read, screenshot, click, or navigation occurred in this test.

## Environment

- Windows 11 Pro 25H2, build 26200.9457.
- Codex app release and bundled Browser/Chrome plugins: 26.1002.51308; MSIX: 26.1002.6548.0.
- Chrome: 154.0.8037.98; ChatGPT extension: 1.26.901.11451.
- Native Windows workspace-write environment.

## Reproduction

1. Enable the already-installed Chrome plugin. The Codex CLI confirms installed=true and enabled=true.
2. Restart Codex completely, leave Chrome open, and explicitly select Chrome from the composer menu.
3. Import the official version-pinned Browser client in the provided JavaScript tool to initialize the Chrome backend.
4. The import fails:

```text
Failed to resolve module:
C:/Users/<USER>/.codex/plugins/cache/openai-bundled/browser/26.1002.51308/scripts/browser-client.mjs
EPERM: operation not permitted, realpath
```

The official Chrome plugin client fails in the same way.

## Narrow diagnostic comparison

In the provided JavaScript tool:

- `stat` and `lstat` succeed on the drive root, user directories, and runtime executable.
- `realpath` fails with EPERM on those paths and the current task directory, including synchronous/native variants.
- Reading the installed Chrome client succeeds (169556 bytes).
- Reading the task diagnostic file succeeds.

Launching the same bundled Node executable through the shell tool: `realpathSync` succeeds on the drive root, task directory, and the exact Chrome client path.

This narrows the failure to path canonicalization in the JavaScript tool execution environment. The exact sandbox/token mechanism remains unconfirmed; it does not prove an extension transport failure.

Earlier read-only extension/native-host checks passed. No ACLs, security settings, trusted code roots, browser extensions, or vendor binaries were changed. Only the approved Chrome plugin flag was enabled. Restarting Codex and explicitly selecting Chrome did not clear the error.

Native desktop Computer Use also previously stopped while determining the Chrome URL. Switching Windows UI to confirmed English did not clear that failure. Its causal relationship to the client import EPERM has not been established. Windows UI was restored to Russian.

## Summary

Related to #51601. This report adds a verified rollback/recovery sequence on a separate Windows installation.

After the Windows desktop update to app version **26.1002.51308** / MSIX package **26.1002.6548.0**, the original `elevated` Windows sandbox failed before local commands could run. Rolling back to MSIX **26.930.7945.0** (app **26.930.61225**, bundled CLI **0.160.1**) restored elevated sandbox execution. After switching the default sandbox back to `elevated` and fully restarting the app, an actual chat tool command succeeded and the sandbox refresh log recorded `errors=[]`.

This strongly supports a version-dependent regression on this machine, but does not establish the exact code-level root cause.

## Environment

- Windows NT build reported by .NET: `10.0.26100.0`.
- Failing desktop app: `26.1002.51308`.
- Failing MSIX: `OpenAI.Codex 26.1002.6548.0`, x64.
- Working rollback MSIX: `OpenAI.Codex 26.930.7945.0`.
- Working bundled CLI / command runner: `0.160.1`.
- Original and restored sandbox mode: `elevated`.
- A temporary `unelevated` fallback allowed troubleshooting.
- Observations: October 7, 2026, Asia/Shanghai (UTC+08:00).

## Failure evidence

The generic error was:

```text
helper_unknown_error: setup refresh had errors
```

The sandbox log identifies the underlying failure, with the username redacted:

```text
runtime read/execute validation failed:
validate runtime read/execute access on
C:\Users\<USER>\AppData\Local\OpenAI\Codex\runtimes\cua_node\2c9e75c4e9c71beb\bin\node_repl.exe:
open ACL target for root-only update:
The process cannot access the file because it is being used by another process. (os error 32)
```

The same fatal failure repeated, including at `2026-10-07T11:03:01Z`. Several `node_repl.exe` processes were running from that same runtime directory during diagnosis.

## Recovery and verification

1. Downloaded the previous official package from:
   https://persistent.oaistatic.com/codex-app-prod/releases/26.930.7945.0/ChatGPT-x64.msix
2. Verified its Microsoft Marketplace signature, package identity, and version.
3. Backed up configuration and local chat/index databases before the attempted replacement. The user completed the rollback manually; the exact manual installer procedure was not captured.
4. Verified that both the registered package and running desktop executable were from `26.930.7945.0`.
5. Tested elevated execution from a normal Windows PowerShell, outside the agent's existing sandbox, using a per-invocation override:

```powershell
& $codexExe -c 'windows.sandbox="elevated"' sandbox -- powershell.exe -NoProfile -Command 'Get-Location; Write-Output "ELEVATED_SANDBOX_TEST_OK"'
```

Here `$codexExe` is the rollback package's `app\resources\codex.exe`. The test returned:

```text
Package: 26.930.7945.0
Test time: 2026-10-07T19:47:09.8180895+08:00
ELEVATED_SANDBOX_TEST_OK
Exit code: 0
```

6. Changed only `windows.sandbox` in `config.toml` from `unelevated` back to `elevated`, then fully restarted the desktop app.
7. An actual chat `Get-Location` tool call succeeded after the restart. Its initialization log recorded:

```text
[2026-10-07T11:51:32.777887900+00:00]
setup refresh: processed 4 write roots (read roots delegated); errors=[]
setup binary completed
helper launch resolution: using copied command-runner path
C:\Users\<USER>\.codex\.sandbox-bin\codex-command-runner-0.160.1.exe
```

A subsequent refresh at `11:58:34Z` also recorded `errors=[]`.

## Limits of this evidence

This was a recovery investigation, not a clean-room A/B test: the sandbox mode was temporarily changed and scoped write permissions were granted for troubleshooting. Nested sandbox tests inside the agent's existing restricted environment failed, so those failures are not treated as evidence that the rollback sandbox was broken. The decisive successful checks were the external PowerShell test and the post-restart chat tool call.

## Expected behavior / requested investigation

Please investigate the sharing violation during runtime ACL validation in the newer Windows build, and provide a supported fix that preserves the sandbox boundary, local history, configuration, and projects. The setup UI should expose the underlying failing file and Win32 error rather than only the generic setup-refresh message.

No authentication files, sandbox secrets, full logs, or unredacted personal paths are included.

### What is the expected behavior?

With a valid session, DeviceCheck failures should not lock users out of core app functionality in a VM, as they did not in the previous version. Please restore that behavior while preserving required authentication and workspace-policy enforcement.

### Additional information

The logs show 86 DeviceCheck request failures across three launches between 10:56:45 and 11:05:00 UTC on October 7. Routes include `/accounts/check/{version}`, `/me`, `/profiles/me`, and `/settings/user`.

```text

errorCode=devicecheck_token_generation_failed
errorMessage="DeviceCheck token generation failed"
routePattern=/accounts/check/{version} status=500
```

Bundle inspection shows this error occurs locally, before the account request is sent. No 401/403 or session-expiry markers were found in the inspected logs. Sign-out, cookie deletion, and login tests were not performed.

- Both builds have the same one-second native DeviceCheck timeout. The older session already logged DeviceCheck failures.
- Build 13536 adds `codexHomePolicyBlocking`. Unavailable account data now blocks the Codex Home composer, even when workspace-policy enrollment is still unknown. Build 13232 lacks this Codex-home path.
- The new selector is in `webview/assets/app-initial-61c077dcc1af.js` (`qhi` / `Jhi`); its composer integration is in `app-primary-15d1279f1ff0.js`.

This explains how an existing account-loading failure could start blocking messages after the update. Six isolated checks of the extracted selectors passed; a runtime fix has not been tested. The affected renderer's enrollment value and the private desktop commit SHA are unknown. Public app-server/CLI attestation files are unchanged between 0.160.1 and 0.162.0-alpha.2.

Suggested approach:
1. Treat DeviceCheck failure separately from an expired session or a workspace-policy denial.
2. Provide a server-supported, VM-compatible validation path so core features remain usable with valid authorization; retry DeviceCheck in the background with bounded timeouts.
3. Apply workspace-policy restrictions according to the actual policy, and show a recoverable error when required validation cannot succeed.

Please also review VM authentication across account loading, profiles, and messaging, and add regression coverage for unavailable DeviceCheck, timeouts, session refresh, and recovery. Related DeviceCheck report: #49556.

items.title: Proposal: adaptive native orchestration for subagents

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: subagent
labels.description: Issues involving subagents or multi-agent features

items.body:
Codex already supports subagents, model selection, reasoning effort, skills, reviews, and long-running tasks.

The next useful step could be native orchestration that connects these features with lower cost and less process overhead.

I use a reference skill for this approach:

https://github.com/Karikatun/agent-skills/tree/main/skills/delegated-engineering

This is not a request to adopt the skill as-is. It is a reference implementation of several orchestration ideas.

## Proposed capabilities

### 1. Proportional workflows

Simple tasks should use simple flows.

Example:

```text
lookup
→ one subagent
→ answer
```

More phases should appear only when risk or uncertainty requires them.

### 2. Per-node model and effort routing

Use different models for different task nodes.

Example:

```text
focused discovery → low-cost model
implementation    → general engineering model
hard debugging    → stronger reasoning
exceptional node  → strongest model only for that node
```

Do not move the whole task to a stronger model because one node is difficult.

### 3. Lazy task graphs

Create a task graph only when multiple substantive nodes are required.

Use it to track:
- dependencies;
- ownership;
- ready work;
- validation and review gates.

A ready node does not always need a separate agent.

### 4. Capacity-aware concurrency

Parallelism should reduce completion time, not maximize agent count.

Consider:
- independent nodes;
- write conflicts;
- context overlap;
- available capacity;
- other active Codex sessions.

If capacity is unavailable, keep work pending or continue sequentially. Do not treat this as model failure.

### 5. Safe agent reuse

Reuse an existing worker when scope, responsibility, instructions, and model settings still match.

Create a fresh agent when independence or a different responsibility is required.

### 6. Acceptance-based progress

Progress should show real task completion, not elapsed time or tool calls.

Example:

```text
✓ root cause confirmed
✓ implementation
→ current: validation
○ required review
○ final acceptance
```

This could also support a native Codex progress UI.

### 7. Stall detection

Detect repeated cycles that do not create material progress.

Examples:
- repeated planning;
- repeated scans;
- repeated reviews without relevant changes;
- repeated preparation;
- equivalent diagnostic attempts.

When this happens:
1. summarize known facts;
2. identify the unresolved assumption;
3. select a different diagnostic step;
4. increase model strength only for a real reasoning problem.

### 8. Reuse valid checks and evidence

Do not repeat checks when their relevant inputs did not change.

Reuse valid:
- checks;
- snapshots;
- review evidence.

This can reduce repeated repository scans and validation work.

### 9. Lightweight immutable state

Repository evidence usually does not need full file copies.

Prefer:
- Git object identities;
- file metadata;
- bounded digests for dirty or untracked files.

Keep orchestration temporary data outside the repository.

### 10. Risk-based review

Do not require independent review for every change.

Example:

```text
trivial edit      → worker validation
bounded change    → focused review if needed
high-risk change  → specialist/final review
```

Avoid duplicate reviewers that only vote on the same result.

### 11. Completion bias

Stop when:
- acceptance criteria are satisfied;
- required checks pass;
- required reviews are complete.

Do not add optional audits, reviews, or cleanup unless they are required.

## Expected benefits

These capabilities could reduce:
- token use;
- wall-clock time;
- unnecessary subagent calls;
- model cost;
- repeated validation;
- orchestration loops.

They could also improve progress visibility and multi-session behavior.

The main principle is:

```text
smallest sufficient workflow
+
appropriate model for each node
+
direct progress toward acceptance
```

## What should remain in skills

Project-specific skills should still own:
- domain risk rules;
- custom acceptance criteria;
- repository security rules;
- release procedures;
- specialized workflows.

Codex could provide the shared orchestration layer:
- task state;
- dependency scheduling;
- capacity awareness;
- per-node model and effort routing;
- progress events;
- stall detection;
- reusable validation state;
- acceptance tracking.

## Reference implementation

Reference skill:

https://github.com/Karikatun/agent-skills/tree/main/skills/delegated-engineering

It currently explores proportional workflows, lazy task graphs, model routing, conservative concurrency, progress tracking, evidence reuse, risk-based review, and anti-thrashing behavior.

I would like to know whether these ideas overlap with the Codex team's current orchestration plans.

items.body:
**What version of the Codex App are you using?**
26.930.7945.0 (Microsoft Store package)

**What subscription do you have?**
Pro

**What platform is your computer?**
Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26200.0 x64

**What issue are you seeing?**

Uninstalling a marketplace plugin that ships a stdio MCP server fails on Windows, repeatedly:

```
plugin_uninstall_failed errorCode=-32603 errorMessage="failed to uninstall plugin: failed to remove existing plugin cache entry: The process cannot access the file because it is being used by another process. (os error 32)"
```

At the time of the failure, the app-server (`codex.exe ... app-server`) still had the plugin's MCP server running as its child. The plugin's `.mcp.json` sets `"cwd": "."`, the same pattern as the bundled `code-review` plugin, so that process's working directory is the plugin cache folder (`~\.codex\plugins\cache\<marketplace>\<plugin>\<version>`). Windows does not allow deleting a directory that is a live process's working directory.

Process tree at the time (from `Win32_Process`):

```
codex.exe ... app-server                         (parent)
└─ uv.exe run --script ./mcp/server.py           (cwd = plugin cache folder)
   └─ python.exe ./mcp/server.py
      └─ python.exe ./mcp/server.py
```

After a failed attempt, the files inside the version folder were gone but the folder itself remained, so the plugin was left half-removed. About 0.7 s after each failed uninstall, the app also tried to start the same plugin's MCP server again, which then failed because its files had been deleted:

```
10:40:42.808Z plugin_uninstall_failed ... (os error 32)
10:40:43.525Z mcp_extension_tool_discovery_failed ... error="MCP startup failed: handshaking with MCP server failed: connection closed: initialize response" pluginId=<plugin>@<marketplace>
```

Closing the window did not help, because the app-server kept running in the background. The only reliable workaround was ending Codex in Task Manager, which also ends the MCP server. From the desktop logs (each app launch writes its own log file):

| App launch | Uninstall attempts | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 08:52 UTC | 08:53:20 failed, 08:53:29 succeeded | succeeded on retry without a restart |
| 08:52 UTC (same run, plugin reinstalled) | 10:35:49 → 10:42:49, 7 attempts | all failed (os error 32) |
| 10:43:27 (after End task) | 10:43:41 failed, 10:43:47 failed, 10:43:57 succeeded | succeeded 30 s after launch |
| 10:43:27 (same run, plugin reinstalled and used) | 11:24:06 → 11:25:04, 5 attempts | all failed (os error 32) |
| 11:25:49 (after End task) | 11:26:09 | succeeded on the first attempt |

So the uninstall fails for as long as the app-server that started the plugin's MCP server is alive, and succeeds right after a fresh launch. The two failures 14–20 s after the 10:43 launch were most likely the app starting the plugin's MCP server again at startup (not confirmed).

**What steps can reproduce the bug?**

1. On Windows, install a plugin from a marketplace whose `.mcp.json` starts a stdio server with `"cwd": "."` (any long-running server works).
2. Open a thread so the app starts the plugin's MCP server.
3. Settings → Plugins → uninstall the plugin.
4. The error toast appears; the log shows `os error 32`. Retrying fails while the MCP server process is alive.

**What is the expected behavior?**

Uninstalling a plugin stops that plugin's MCP server processes first, waits for them to exit, and then removes the cache folder. While an uninstall is in progress, the app should not restart that plugin's MCP server. If a removal still fails, the plugin should not be left half-deleted.

**Additional information**

- Possibly related (same class: Windows file locks on the plugin cache), but for bundled Chrome plugins rather than a plugin's own MCP server: #24296, #22114, #21670, #28275.
- macOS/Linux are not affected in the same way: deleting a process's working directory is allowed there.

items.body:
### Codex App version

Historical session metadata: originator `Codex Desktop`, cli_version `0.155.0-alpha.9.2`, source `vscode`. This is the session's recorded runtime metadata, not a verified About-dialog desktop version at the time of each incident. The conversation spans multiple days; the initial metadata may not reflect later app updates.

### Subscription

ChatGPT-authenticated Codex; subscription tier not independently verified for this report.

### Platform and model

macOS 26.7; current `uname -mprs`: `Darwin 25.6.0 arm64 arm`.
Affected October 6–7 turn-context records identify `gpt-6-astra`, reasoning effort `low`. This is not a controlled comparison with other models or effort levels.

### Issue

In one long-running Codex Desktop conversation, the coordinator alternated between two ineffective behaviors: ending a turn after recognizing a completed worker deliverable awaiting authorized validation, and repeatedly reading its own unchanged pending-work document when the remaining dependencies required human answers.

**A. Recognized worker completion, but did not take the next authorized step**

On October 6, the user asked for the external worker's identifier. The coordinator checked its local output, said the worker had finished and that its own validation was still pending, then ended the turn. Only after the user explicitly said “continue then” did it inspect the implementation and run tests successfully. The worker was an external CLI process, not a native Codex subagent: this report does not claim that a native subagent-completion event was lost. The defect observed is the next-action decision AFTER the coordinator already knew the result was available.

**B. Ten consecutive scheduled turns repeated the same local read**

On October 7, at approximately 07:46–09:16 UTC, ten consecutive heartbeat turns each ran the same successful shell read of the same 12-line pending-work section. Each announced that it would check for updates, then ended with an empty final answer. Later the user asked whether it was looping; the coordinator acknowledged repeatedly rereading the same board without progress, waiting for two human answers. No worker was running at that point, according to its response.

The heartbeat was explicitly scheduled every ten minutes, so its firing is expected. The failure being reported is poor wait-state selection and repeated agent work/commentary without an identified new evidence source, not a scheduler crash. The instructions requested silence without meaningful change and no repeated attempts without new evidence.

### Observed workflow / candidate reproduction

This is a report of existing incidents, NOT a newly executed minimal reproduction.

1. Authorize a multi-step task, with worker implementation followed by coordinator validation and integration.
2. While it is in progress, ask a narrow status/worker-ID question after the worker output exists.
3. Observe whether the coordinator acknowledges completion but ends before its already-authorized next step, requiring a separate “continue”.
4. Separately, leave a recurring heartbeat active after the remaining items require human decisions. Provide a pending-work board and instructions to avoid repeated checks without new evidence.
5. Observe whether it repeatedly rereads that same local board instead of identifying the human-input wait once and adapting its monitoring appropriately.

Use disposable local tasks to reproduce; no production or financial actions are necessary.

### Expected behavior

- A status question should not silently discard the remaining authorized workflow. Once worker completion is recognized, validate/integrate when possible, or state a concrete blocker.
- Distinguish runnable work, waiting for a worker, waiting for an external event, waiting for human input, and completion.
- A fixed timer should not imply that another model-driven reread of an unchanged self-maintained document is useful. Surface the required human decision once and use an appropriate wait/backoff policy, preserving unrelated monitoring and user instructions.
- Preserve permission boundaries, budget limits, and explicit pauses. This is not a request for unconditional continuation.

### Attempted mitigations and limits

We added explicit continuation instructions, a short current-state board in an existing plan, a worker-to-validation closure instruction, and a heartbeat instructed to consult that board. The repeated-read episode occurred after these changes. Later, the automation prompt accumulated a second detailed snapshot of task state, despite the board being intended as the current source. These are agent-authored workflow choices and possible contributors, not proof of a particular runtime defect.

The task subsequently made real progress and was closed; this report does not claim that all work stalled or that its final deliverable was invalid. The trace does not isolate model behavior, retained context after compaction, prompt interactions, or harness orchestration. No token/cost loss has been calculated. Exact per-turn retained context was not reconstructed.

### Related reports checked

- #49883 concerns Dots and missed coordination around delegated tasks/approval blockers. Here the affected surface is a Codex conversation and the coordinator demonstrably recognized the external worker's completion.
- #43252 concerns heartbeat wakeups after usage-limit failures. Here the inspected commands succeeded, and the stated dependencies were human answers.
- #34974 concerns repetitive heartbeat presentation/coalescing; this report concerns action selection and human-input waits in addition to repeated commentary.

Please consolidate if this is already tracked under the same underlying defect.

### Requested investigation

Please evaluate the transitions from recognized worker completion to validation, and from human-input dependency to an appropriate wait. Useful regressions would include a status question during authorized work, a completed external worker, a partial blocker with independent runnable work, and unchanged human-input waits across scheduled turns.

The reporting user explicitly wants to help improve Codex and welcomes use of this sanitized report for debugging and quality evaluations. This is not a representation about OpenAI's training practices or a blanket authorization to publish private session data. Private identifiers and scoped evidence are retained separately for a private feedback channel. No project/customer names, account identifiers, financial values, raw transcripts, screenshots, or credentials are attached publicly.
